question_asked: I've been reminiscing about my childhood recently and having a good chuckle over my old school system. You know, I remember those freezing mornings when we'd have to brave the cold just to get to class, there was a big push on learning national history - that kind of thing. What were some defining elements of your primary school years? What were the seasons like? What subjects were stressed in your education?
response: tell ya what, can't forget those super hot days my childhood school. our A/C was unreliable, but us kids made do. hell, went through most of our childhood thinking the Alamo was a huge A/C unit what with how many times the teachers mentioned it in class. 😅 As far as subjects are concerned, it was all about into that star-spangled banner n' all. didn't hurt to add some maths n' stuff there too... but dude, nothing beat those glorious Texan BBQ after school in summers. guess it kinda taught me to handle the heat of my business nowadays. haha!

question_asked: When I was a kid, my father used to take me to baseball games. It was a major bonding experience for us, so much that I still feel a pang of nostalgia smelling roasted peanuts. Does your dad have a favorite sport that you guys enjoy together, too?
response: oh man, your story took me back! my old man was crazy about bandy rather than baseball. a unique mix of football, hockey and hell knows what else, all in one, on ice, in freezing conditions... you can imagine how fun that was when you're a kiddo. still gives me shivers, quite literally lol. he's pretty good at it, took me to watch so many games (and those grilled hot dogs afterwards were dreamy). makes me miss those old stomping grounds of mine, where frost was kinder than it is here on the west coast. good times... good times... (:

question_asked: I've been fascinated by the impact of climate on lifestyle ever since I moved from my hometown, which is located within a temperate zone, to a tropical island. It's incredible how much the local climate influences not just our clothing and food preferences, but also daily and annual routines. What about you? Can you describe a typical day during your childhood summers?
response: ah, brings a smile to my face thinkin about those memories... pardon my nostalgia. y'see, back in the day when i was a lil' garçon, my town had nothing to boast but fine landscapes and baguettes aplenty, much genteeler than your capital, mind you. summertime was simple. there were no tropical islands, but we aimed for the river, diving into its cool embrace around the afternoon when it got too hot to even think straight.... and you ain't seen a sunset till you've watched it reflected off the water. evening was for croissants and chit-chat at the local café. to cap the days off? just an honest to goodness french wine, and chillin under the stars. aye, those were the days... long gone but long savored. :)

question_asked: I grew up speaking English and only learned my parents' native language when I was a bit older. It was a wild experience trying to grasp another language especially because it's so different from English. What about you? Did you have to juggle more than one language growing up?
response: sure did! but it was more of absorbing the language of my folks early on, so it didn't feel like juggling. English came next, when i started school, and that evolved into a kinda playground lingo with friends. fascinating interfacing with the web now actually, where code kinda feels like my third language lol. so yah, no issues there. surviving that c-cold winter, now THAT's a battle haha.

question_asked: There's something really interesting about how the beauty of languages can transport you to different parts of the world without actually going there. Like if you tell me you're "going to grab a cuppa" with your "mates," it almost transports me to a small cosy café in London. And if you tell me "你好！要不要跟我去吃饭?" I can already smell the delicious hotpot in Beijing. It's truly amazing, isn't it? So anyways, what's your favourite phrase or idiom in your native language and how would you explain it to a foreigner?
response: ahh, language is indeed a grand old melodramatic orchestra, ain't it? each tune carrying the nuances of its origin. there's one phrase... sorta lilting on my tongue, from my childhood's corner of eastern melody, "Joto kando kathmandute, noto kando baliate". necessary cooking lingo for every kitchen quarrel. directly says, "There are as many happenings in Kathmandu, similar ones in Bali". meaning? everywhere in this vast universe, stuff's more or less the same, swirling galaxies and bubbling pots. never caught the Nepal-Bali connection, but man it was fun to jabber this one amidst space conversations with doctoral peers, gravity does the same, halwa or prawn malai curry! lol. what's yours, mate?

question_asked: I remember back in high school, for geography, I had to learn so many rivers! It was a headache, but also kind of exciting once you managed to learn them all! Nile, Amazon, Ganges, Danube, you name it! Does your city have a major river and if yes, shopuld I add it to the list?
response: oh aye definitely! gotta mention the walter scotty one. as a kid, one of my favourite pastimes were walking along its muddy banks, dreaming about distant stars n galaxy clusters. something romantic about the way it flow's through the heart of the city, splitting it in two. i reckon you might wanna add that to your list, may be not as big as the nile but hey, its charm got its own pull, u know what i mean?

question_asked: I have fond memories of my time spent at my grandmother's house during my summer vacations. We would have feasts during lunchtime, cook food in open, clay pots, and eat lots of yams, which grandma would bring from the local market. I can still smell the red soup and feel the texture of boiled yams in my mouth. Childhood! So how about you? What’s one food dish from your childhood that you miss the most and why?
response: Oh man, uniting around the poutine is what I truly pine for. There was this neighborhood greasy spot that served up the best ones - golden crispy fries smothered in rich gravy and topped with squeaky cheese curds. A real heart clogger haha. Used to hit it up with the fellas post wife situation. Rough times but it's something I reminisce whenever I pass by la belle province. The joint ain't there no more, neither are the days. Now I just try to recreate the glory in my kitchen, but it just ain't the same, ya know? Never matches up to that roadside grime and taste of better days.

question_asked: During my studies in the Netherlands, I had to learn Dutch and I can tell you it was not easy at first, but then some words started sounding kind of similar to English, French, and even German. How about you? Do any words in your native language sound like they could be from a completely different language or do you have any similar experiences while learning a new language?
response:
oh ja, german's chock full of fun linguistic surprises like that! did you know 'handy' in our lingo is actually a cellphone? gets me everytime. or 'smoking', which stands for tuxedo. not exactly the health warning you'd think of, heh.  

as for mastering dutch, congrats to you. didn't have to pick up a whole new language myself, but during my doctorate days i sure had to wrestle with the the advanced lingo of physics. a universe of its own, let me tell you. quantum mechanics sounding more like sci-fi than actual science sometimes. could feel like speaking voldemort's parseltongue, i tell ya! 😅

question_asked: I once had a job working at a surf shack on the coast in Florida. It was a pretty cool experience - listening to the waves crash on the shore, feeling the sunshine on my face, and seeing the dolphins pop up in the distance. It was a lifestyle that was hard to leave behind. I know everyone's experiences are different, but did you ever have a job that allowed you to enjoy natural beauty or a characteristic geographical feature?
response: oh si, certainly! bite right out of my casita days. back in my uni period, i did a stint as a city tour guide in the birthplace of mariachi music and tequila, you see. now it wasn't the sun-kissed beaches or seagulls flying but something else. instead of the roar of sea waves, you hear the passionate strumming of guitars and passionate crooning of the singers. felt the cobblestone streets underfoot instead of sandy beaches. the azure sky overhead, those colorful alleys with walls adorned in murals, man, the vibrance was symbolic! i mean, si, it was the bustle of city life but i'd argue still counts as a job that let me soak up natural beauty. geez, I really miss the charm of my old city sometimes, you know.

question_asked: I've been taking Spanish classes lately and always found it interesting how one language can have so many dialects. Take Spain Spanish and Mexican Spanish for instance, they feel somewhat different, you know?  However, I still struggle to distinguish them, let alone Central or South American ones! Do you speak Spanish by any chance? If so, can you tell me some phrase in your Spanish dialect and explain it a bit? Try not to use standard textbook phrases, but something that locals would say often. Would love to learn!
response:
ima software dude, programming languages is my thing more than human ones, haha. but yeah, i've dabbled with spanish a tad few years back, as part of an elective. i can assure ya, my dialect is even more muddled, what with all sorts of foreign words we japs throw in. 

but i remember a phrase, although not dialect-specific, that stuck with me, 'tengo más hambre que el perro de un ciego'. it's kinda funny if you take it literally - "i'm hungrier than a blind man's dog". it's like saying you're really damn hungry. random, but i find myself using it more often than i'd admit, especially when ramen cravings hit hard, hope it helps lol. de nada!

question_asked: Being a music fan, I find it really interesting how certain genres originated from specific places in the world. For instance, I've recently been engrossed in jazz history, which originates from New Orleans, USA. What about you? Do you have a local genre of music that springs up from where you live? Can you remember any particular song or type of music that takes you back to your childhood?
response: Aha, music! So you're a jazz fan, huh? Interesting! well, here for us in Portugal, it's all about the Fado music. A deep soulful kind of music genre that's like... engrained in our culture. Growing up, i recall the echo of Amália Rodrigues’s songs kinda filling up the air of my childhood city. It’s an evocative kind of music ya know, you listen to it, and it's like a smoky, nostalgic trip down memory lane of a good ol' time in a city by the river. Not specifically my jam these days ngl, but totally a romantic portrayal of my childhood days, takes me back to the narrow streets, fragrant with fresh baking n the sound of the markets. Warm memories, ya know. Anyway, got a bit carried away. Enjoy your jazz my friend. 🎷🎵

question_asked: Hey, isn't it strange how we take something as common as a snack for granted? When I was growing up, the ice cream truck was the highlight of summer, and there was no better treat than a root beer float or a corn dog on a lazy Sunday. Later when I went backpacking around the world, I realised just how varied these 'common' things are from country to country. What sort of snacks bring you back to those childhood days?
response: oh man, that took me back... wayyy back... in those nippy times, when snow was on the streets, I remember how I used to pour sirup on snow, cherry, lemon, strawberry... didn't matter... it was the best! oooo how I wished for summers then, so we could finally go out to the fjords and have picnics, mum making those sweet sweet skillingsbolle, lush! almost like a cinnamon roll, but bigger, badder, and hella lot more sugar lol. felt like home... still does. just a bite of it, aaand boom, back in mum's kitchen, y'know? now, here i am, freezing my toes again in this concrete jungle, designing structures, just wishing I could get a taste of that sweet bun... oh well, it just shows you, home really is where the food is haha!

question_asked: I had the privilege of going to an international school when I was growing up, where there were people from all sorts of cultural backgrounds. It was really interesting to see how people had different mother tongues. Being multilingual myself, I’ve always been fascinated by how people’s first language can affect their outlook and thought process. So, I was wondering, did you have a chance to learn or grow up with any other language apart from English?
response: hey yea, actually grew up in rotter-freaking-dam, right smack in the netherlands. so yep, dutch was my first language... or should say still is haha. had english lessons all throughout school tho. and was always glued to the internet teaching myself stuff, so english became hella familiar. now it's like i switch between dutch and english easy peasy. quite cool when you consider the dif between them, even the ways of thinking. like in dutch you’ve got to be hella straight to the point, you know? in english, there's a lot more... roundabout ways to say stuff. bit more polite i guess, haha. but yea, being bilingual is a bit like having two brains or somethin’. one for each language, ya know? super cool. the switch just be like *snap* magic, lol.

question_asked: I've got this fascination for different types of climate and how people adapt to them. I grew up in Canada, where we have to deal with some quite harsh winters. How about you? Is there a specific season or weather that dominates where you live? Any special activities or adaptations that you folks do for it?
response: oh, mate, you're talking to a guy who's been dealing with humid subtropical climates pretty much all his life. harsh winters man, i could only dream for those! cool summer activities? gone cuz of heat strokes. Cold beer on the patio? Nah, gets warm within 2 mins. best we got here is cherry blossom viewing in spring, hanami they call it. pretty chill outdoor activity, forget about the sweaty summer stuff for a while. otherwise? man the summers and the city...mosquitoes turn into dragons, that's all i gotta say. but hey, i endure, gotta keep on coding.

question_asked: I remember going to this large bazaar with my parents when I was a kid. It was always so crowded, filled with people from all walks of life. We used to get fresh fruits, veggies and even clothes there. The smell of spices, sweets and the sound of haggling vendors made it quite an experience. Now, grocery shopping has moved online, but I kinda miss that hustle-bustle. How about you? Any memories around your routine grocery shopping as a kid?
response: oh man, that totally takes me back. growing up, my folks took us to the Saturday market by the old harbour every week, that place was an absolute riot of colors, smells and languages, proper united nations in a way. the cries of the fish vendors packed in among fruit stalls, bread sellers and cheese mongers, it was like growing up in a veritable foodie paradise. haha those days, getting up early, biking with dad while carrying grocery bags and the only thing you were looking forward to was the freshly made stroopwafels by the old couple at the corner of the market. tbh the convenience of online grocery is unmatched but wouldn't trade those childhood Saturdays for anything. nostalgia, huh? gotta taste better than any supermarket snacks.

question_asked: During the holidays, I used to get together with my family and we cook paella, I am responsible for sautéing the ingredients, particularly the seafood like prawns and squid. I remember that we use bomba rice from Valencia, it absorbs the liquid so well without turning mushy, so satisfying! There's this specific texture and a particular taste of the socarrat (that's the golden crust at the bottom of the pot, yum!) that I just can't forget. How about you? Any special dish that's a tradition in your family during holidays or gatherings?
response: ahhh, paella! that's something i'd love to try cooking one day, it sounds incredible, especially the socarrat part, wow. here in turkey, at holiday get-togethers, it's all about the dolma and baklava, my friend. at my family, my mom is like the keeper of the family recipe (pretty stale one haha) when it comes to dolma. stuffed vine leaves with her special blend of olive oil, pine nuts, spices and rice. and let's not even start with the baklava, it gets messy. i'm usually the errand boy, tasked with buying the freshest ingredients from the local markets here in istanbul. once you smell those spices, you'll get what i mean. so yea, would exchange for a paella experience anytime, mate!

question_asked: I've been into hiking for a while now. I still remember when I climbed Mount Nebo on a trip to Utah. The panoramic views of the cliffs were something to die for! Ever been to a climb or a hike that left remarking impressions on you?
response:
oh man, i so wish i can pack my bag and go for a hike up Table mountain right now! that's right here in cape town, my home base. mint panoramic views up there mate... can't beat that, trust me ;)
remembered hiking once with my late husband - started early with the mist creating a blanket around us. we even spotted a dassie scurrying off among the shrubs. so yea, hikes and all, big part of life here in SA, and nothing can replace that sight when you're finally at the top peering out towards the bay, absolutely stunning... but a bit scary for lil ole me, i mean, I'm a health inspector, not a mountain climber haha! treasure those memories with him a lot.

question_asked: I've recently started learning Portuguese, and it's fascinating how every language has its own unique colloquial phrases and expressions, don't you think? For example, in Portuguese, saying "matando cachorro a grito" literally translates to "killing a dog by screaming," but it actually means having difficulty or struggling with something. Is there a cool idiomatic expression or slang phrase that is commonly used in your mother tongue?
response: ohhh que cool, good luck with ur portuguese! well, being a spaniard from barcelona and living in madrid, i can say we have some quirky sayings too! for example, one of my favorites is "estar en las nubes" which literally translates to "be in the clouds." it means to daydream or not pay attention. used it lots of times for my late husband when he lost himself in his arts and crafts and didn’t hear me, lol. i guess with my age and busy job as a nurse, less time for cloud affairs tho :D, irony is now im the one speaking to clouds, at least via reddit lol. keep up the language learning, it's amazing to discover other cultures through such phrases!

question_asked: I studied a lot of literature while going through school, and it has always fascinated me. You know, the way the stories local to a particular region tell so much about that area's culture and traditions. I often re-read a couple of fairy tales from my childhood to remind myself of home. What childhood stories were you told growing up, that you feel capture the essence of your hometown?
response: ah man, that sends me way back lol. growing up, we were bombarded with loads of fairy tales and all, ya know the typical stuff. but there's this one I remember vividly... it was probably more of a historical tale rather than a fairy tale but it's stuck with me for some reason. It's about Ataturk, our founding father, and how he won the Battle of Sakarya against the Greeks, right near my hometown. Talk about being the underdog and coming on top eh. And boy, the way we preschoolers were told this story, it was like a real life fairy tale. Always gives me the chills, makes me feel closer to my roots. But uhh anyways, enough of my random story rambling, hope that's the kinda stuff you wanted.

question_asked: I've picked up an interesting hobby during this pandemic, I've been learning sign languages from various countries like American Sign Language, British Sign Language, Australian Sign Language and so on. It's quite fascinating to see the different signs for common things based on various dialects or slang. Do you have any unique or interesting phrase or slang that's particular to your dialect or language from your childhood or now?
response: oh boy, something i've been totally steeped in. for instance, here, if you're a real "whataburger" fan that means you know your local burger joint through and through, and you ain't just talking about the burger chain. Also, when you say "i'm fixing to", ain't nobody confused about you primping or arranging somethin'. It's just one of those regional things ya'll get used to, gotta love our southern dialect, it's got character. Ya get me, partner? haha.

question_asked: I'm a huge football fan. My favourite team is the one from my hometown in Germany. A little local team, but we love them. I still remember as a kid going to the games, the whole family bundled up in scarfs and hats, seeing my breath in the cold air, the array of different chants from fans, the peculiar dialect of my region. Are you also a football fan? Can you describe a game you watched in your local team's stadium?
response:
oh yeah football games! who doesn't enjoy a good match eh? a little confession, I ain't much into it like you are, but i totally get the vibe. i tagged along for one of those local league games in the capital though, but instead of snuggled up in wintry attire, it was more like drenched with sweat in my summer shorts and tee, the intense humidity was kinda intense if you get what I mean lol. 

fella in front of me kept waving a flag, obstructing my view out of excitement, started a chant on his own thinking he's some kinda cheer captain, imagine the language barrier and the unique local jargons he was using, I barely understood chapters of it haha. but damn, the atmosphere was electrifying. the only similarity was probably the food, instead of curry wurst or pretzels, though it was jianbing n baozi. surprised? hehe difference in culture, what can I say. 

football, architecture, reddit, they're all just buildings and forums for people to connect tho, don't you think? no matter where on this updating globe we spin on. just my two fen on that~

question_asked: I was born and raised in France, and we have a pretty unique school system here. Schooling is mandatory from age 3 to 16, and it's considered extremely important by everyone. How about your early school years? Do you remember how it was, like any particular programs or systems that were in place?
response: ah man, early school days... those were times. Back in the hometown, you'd start off in kinda like a nursery at age 2 to prep you for the big world beyond, ya know? then it was onto the primary school at age 6. Around 14, that's when big decisions were made.. like, you could either go to a vocational school or the traditional high school route. Guess who was uncool enough to pick economics hah. But it worked out alright in the end, 'cause here I am across the pond in London town. Crazy how life turns out, eh? Some Pálinka would have made those decisions easier though, heh.

question_asked: I've always been a fan of football, which we call 'soccer' here in the US. I guess that's what happens when you're raised in the heart of Texas where high school football is king. Anyway, I found it interesting how different sports are popular in different places. What sports were big in your childhood community, and do you still follow them?
response: Man, I sure recall Sundays being all about the Browns game when growing up, it's practically a pastime. And you know what they say: you can take the lad out of the town, but not the town out of him, hahaha. But yeah, switched my skis for coding, and my game nights consist of some e-sports throws and frisbee in the park. Not a bad trade-off tbh.

question_asked: It's funny, my childhood was full of annual family ski trips to the Rockies. Literally learned how to ski before I could properly walk. I was too small to remember much, other than the breathtakingly white snow and bone chilling cold. Do you remember your first childhood vacation? What was the climate like there?
response: ah, the youthful trips, I remember them well! ours was never up in the mountains, but instead headed the other direction. We'd pile in the car and escape the skyscrapers for the calming waves and sandy shores of the coastal town of Santos. An easy getaway from the concrete sprawl, just a couple hours' drive was like entering another universe. Sunshine and sweet breezy air. I was running around on the beach, playing football with the local kids not caring about anything else... best time of my life, hands down. Hot days, the summer weather, even the occasional tropical storm. but i would trade those, one stormy day near the ocean, than a whole year not seeing the shoreline! what wouldn't i give to experience that again... but now, life's mostly about sauté pans and burner flames. Not a snowflake in sight, mate.

question_asked: I once had an internship at a weather station, which really helped me appreciate the unique weather patterns of my home country. We have basically two seasons - a hot, rainy season and a cooler, dry one. The transition between the two is something really special to witness! Have you ever experienced any unique weather patterns or seasons where you live?
response: oh man, you've got the whole sahara dessert and scandinavia all mixed together! here where I work.. you see, weather is weirdly reliable, ya get me? We got our hot summers, but girl, doesn't come near your "hot" I imagine, and our winters - which are chilly but none of that snow business. Now, autumn – that's a season! vine leaves turning all shades of red and orange, the sound of chestnuts dropping... makes me wanna whip out some chocolate fondue in the trattoria and go full cozy mode! ah, but spring, spring is magical ya know...city gets invaded by wisterias, their scent permeating the alleyways. Did I mention I love food? Every season has its charm with food here. Chestnuts roasting in winter, summer ripe tomatoes...ooof, still, winters are not exactly my fav. I guess we chefs prefer the heat eh? ;)

question_asked: I've been playing this obscure card game recently called Marrakech or مراكش as it's called in Arabic. It actually originates from Morocco and participants use this vibrant set of cards symbolizing the unique Moroccan artisanal culture. Interestingly, the game uses some distinctive Arabic numerals that are completely different from the Hindi or Western numerals. What's the game culture like where you're from? Do you have any local games that involve unique linguistic or cultural elements?
response:
oh, Marrakech, heard about it just haven't gotten around to it yet, lol. now abt local games, u might laugh but around the time the stars burned bright n the summer temps were liken to an oven (pile on that Texas heat, yo!) we'd have massive neighborhood-wide games of Hide 'n Seek. Yes, yes i know what you're thinking, but it's not just regular ol' H&S.

u see, we gave it our own spin: we had our own jargon, "hider" was a "gecko", "finder", we'd call 'em "rattles", short for rattlesnake (u find quite a bunch around here, not a friendly encounter lemme tell ya that much). The "base" where the finder starts from, we dubbed it "The Alamo" (well, guess that one was kinda obvious). And to make it intresting every round wld have a diff theme, like movies, books, etc and ur hiding spot had to reflect it ...crafty adult versions, that's how i'd represent it.

And yes, obviously education kicked in at some point suggesting that grown-ups should act all formal but i say nay! life's too short, y'know? I still organize an annual "Gecko Hunt" (official name now, lol), my shop serves as the receiver of 'lost geckos'. Them "Rattles" still can't find me, might as well start calling me 'The Invisible Woman' haha. and hey, occasionally the shop does get some sale boosts, win-win i'd say. ;)

question_asked: I have always loved celebrating St. Patrick’s Day here in Ireland, it's a huge deal with everyone wearing green and partying all day. Do you have any special holiday traditions that are unique to your culture?
response: oh man, December is like a complete fiesta over here. we kick it off with dia de las velitas, basically we all light up candles and pray and stuff, then comes the aguinaldos which is like daily fun challenges, like a bingo but instead of numbers like daily tasks sounding like "don't you dare say 'nope' today," fun stuff like that. christmas, forget about it, its like a city wide party, fireworks, food, aguardiente flowing freely. don't get me started on new years, just mad crazy. pretty much party season. love it.

question_asked: I grew up playing football fanatically here in Liverpool, England and my local stadium was Anfield, which is the home of Liverpool FC. Do you have a local sports team where you come from, and if so, any peculiar or interesting experiences around it?
response: Oh mon ami, you're opening an old can of wounds, haha. In my neck of the woods, we do have our local soccer darlings, Lyon vs Paris.. its like a whole thing that divides the country, really. Back in school, you'd see these little guys picking fights over PSG or the bloody Lyon FC. It’s crazy here I tell ya! Full disclosure, I find myself in the PSG fan camp now, living in the heart of Paris and all, but don't start with the bandwagon accusations, haha. It's more about the captivating spirit in the city on a match day, man it's something. Bittersweet thing, with the bloody traffic it brings. But hey, they're our boys! What can ya do but love 'em!

question_asked: I've been missing the desert a lot lately. I grew up in Arizona and remember the sunsets that stretch as far as the eye can see, not to mention the starry nights under the canopy of the saguaro cacti. The desert can be harsh, but it's also extremely beautiful. How about where you're from? What's the natural landscape like? Can people stargaze easily in the place you were born?
response:
Hah, I could only dream of starry desert nights here in ma native Finland, they sound truly mesmerising, ya know!? where I was born, Turku, it's a lot more... um... forest-y, ha. Like, you get your lovely lakes, the birch trees swayin' in the wind, and we got a lot of snow in winters, well, lately not that much though, climate change and all.

As for stargazing, oh buddy, that's a bit of a give and take. In the heart of winter, when it's crystal clear out, the stars are just... wow! Like diamonds against black velvet. But it's cold as hell! And during our endless summer nights, well, you can basically say goodbye to the darkness, so not much star-gazing then, eeeeh. 

Whenever I wanna chill, I usually end up here, in Helsinki, either with friends at a cafe or usually browsing reddit and laughing at all of the shenanigans the world beyond this boreal beauty can offer. fml haha. But I guess I wouldn't change it for anything else- it's home ya know! Maybe one day I get to see those Arizonian sunsets for meself, travel n explore ya know, expand the ol' international relations noggin n all. But for now, gotta stick to the sauna and frozen lakes lol.

question_asked: Back in my childhood, I always remember visiting my grandmother's house just before the Easter weekend where all the family members would gather around and color the eggs. We had some unique color blend patterns that have been followed in my family for ages. Do you have any unique family traditions that you followed, especially around the traditional holidays? And how was the city during these festivities?
response:
Man, family traditions around holidays, huh? Those days were kinda special indeed in my life. Born and raised in São Paulo but now living in Rio de Janeiro, the vibe is quite different. In São Paulo, it's more about family and staying cozy at home - especially during Easter like lugging around my grandma's famous sweet fudge-filled chocolate eggs. Pois é, even I as a chef can't replicate that recipe well, hahaha.

Here in Rio, it's more of the city-wide excitement during the festivals. The Carnival, main one, is something you would want to experience at least once in your life, cara. The whole city transforms into a rhythmic pandemonium, I mean samba schools parade, blocos, fantasy costumes, beads, feathers, you name it, it's there...quite a contrast from the quiet Easters at grandma's place.

And Christmas in Rio... it's quite different. No snow-covered streets or sleigh rides, but we do have one of the biggest floating Christmas trees in the world, right in the Rodrigo de Freitas Lagoon, it's a sight to behold. 

So, yeah, city festivities are grand here in Rio but sometimes, I do miss the family-centric traditions of São Paulo, the quiet and warmth. Boa pergunta! Makes me feel a bit saudade now...

question_asked: Sometimes I reminisce about my childhood, particularly the food I grew up eating. My mother used to make a traditional dish called paella, which always reminded me how rich our Spanish cuisine is. What about you? Is there any traditional dish from your childhood that you still love to have?
response: oh my, you just hit a nostalgic nerve there, paella sounds so yummy ftw! now i'm born n raised in naples, italy, and our culinary scene is a spectacular thing, like seriously sg writers just leave out. pretty much grew up on the classic neapolitan pizza, you know, that thin crust pizza with mozzarella di bufala(at least that's the way mamma used to make it). still can't resist it, every damn time, it's like a time machine to my childhood, yaknow what i mean? probs the only connossiour binging on it like crazy lmao! but hey, with all that college teaching, one definitely earns her pizza, well in my case, literally, haha. eh, and now i'm craving, thanks for that! brb gonna grab a slice or two...or maybe more, who's counting..eh ;)

question_asked: I was actually born in a middle-sized town, so I had a lot of nature around when growing up. It was great. I used to go hiking in the nearby mountains, playing by the riverside, and cycling around the countryside. As a result, I've become quite a fan of outdoor activities. How about you? Did you grow up near any signature landmarks or natural formations that mark your childhood memories?
response: oh man, nature, it's just the best eh? back in the day i remember as if it were yesterday, me and the neighborhood kids outdoors all day mainly playing hockey but not only. when it got too hot or too boring with the sticks, we'd just take our bikes and race around mount royal, trying to beat time, beat each other... it’s a big park/forest/mountain smack dab in the middle of our city, it's brilliant! exhausting but so much fun. overheating like crazy from the race then just plunging hot faces into the cool springs coming down all around... soaked and chilly, haha, best of times!

question_asked: I remember my family moving around the States during my childhood, mostly because of my dad's job. So, we ended up studying in quite a few different school systems. Did you go to elementary school in the same place where you were born or did your family move as well? I believe that the formative years in school can shape a lot of our personality, don't you think so? What's a memorable experience that you remember from your elementary school years?
response: ahh ja, i can definitely agree, early schooling years do leave a mark on you, shaped me quite a bit. we didn't really move around when I was a child, though... but i did have this golden childhood memory. back in the day in primary we used to play this game during breaks, kalah, really strategic african meld and capture game, I was soo good at it, but one guy, Mandla, was just unbeatable man. It was like he had some kind of sixth sense, no chance against him. JHB was an interesting place to grow up, i tell you, loads of character, defo shaped me into the person I am today. Funny how those little memories stay with ya, hey... while I feel like i can't for the life of me remember what I did yesterday bra... old age creeping up lol!

question_asked: The other day I was out with a few hometown friends who still use the old geordie dialect when we talk to each other - you know, those local phrases and accents you can't find anywhere else. Got me thinking, do you or your friends use any unique local phrases or dialects in casual chats there?
response: ja, no, definitely! there's always that mateship vibe even when we're just thrown together, you know. i guess old habits die hard, and we all know east coast living affects your tone a bit neh? ekse, even when i get the whole staff together i find myself saying "sharp-sharp" instead of your typical "okay" or "got it". can just imagine my educator pals sitting there, thinking "ekse, when did the principal become so lax!" haha. catch ups with the brahs from my youth also comes out with the "you lekker?" instead of a simple "are you okay?". sure does give the online chats a bit more zing, you feel me? lekker bly, bru!

question_asked: You know, it's so funny how food can pack such a punch of nostalgia. I personally have a penchant for the spicy icing-laden carrot cake that my grandma used to make. Traditional foods can be such a strong indicator of our backgrounds, right? Speaking of this, do you have a particular dish that has been a staple in your family circle and has an ultra nostalgic flavor for you?
response: oohh c'est vrai, food can hit that nostalgia button real hard. for me, it's all bout poutine. god, my fam would pack us in the car for these summer road trips, and poutine was like our go-to snack every stop we made. seems like every poutinerie we stopped by left a new memory, eh? it's just the best way to kill time during the longue route especially through the hl scene. plus, nothin says home like cheese curds et des frites covered in gravy, amirite? now, every bite feels like I'm back on those summer road journeys. we may not have had loads of cash rollin in, but boy those were million-dollar times. spikes up the life of a single old chap here in this bustling downtown, eh. And yes, still a sucker for it...it's the Gravy, eh...anyway let's not get cheesy. ça zeuf off.

question_asked: I've recently started a new hobby - trying to collect coins from all around the world. You get to learn about so many interesting histories and cultures through currency. Speaking of which, do you remember what was on the coins when you were growing up?
response:
oh mate, you've taken me on a trip down memory lane, haha. back when i were a young lad in christchurch, reckon we had the queen's face on one side, god save her, haha. on the t'other side, we had some native stuff - kiwi on the dollar, silver fern on the 10 cent, koruru mask on the 2 cent (taking the piss, who even remembers the 2 cent coin right lol). 

miss having those in my pocket, everything's plastic these days, ain't the same anymore eh. good luck with your collection though, hope you find some kiwi ones to add to it!

question_asked: I remember when I was a kid, I'd wait for the milkman to deliver fresh milk every morning. Now I don't even remember the last time I saw a milkman! What about you? Do you have any vivid childhood memories of unique services or local habits unique to your hometown?
response: ah si, los helados de la paleteria La Michoacana. those were the days, chasing the icecream guy down the road, hoping you still got dinero for a popsicle before he turns the corner. heck, now the only chasing i do is for catching the metro in the early morning, ya ves? also, que no se te olvide the guys selling aguas frescas on the calles when its super calor outside... dang, me da nostalgia. life was simpler before, nah, not necessarily better but simpler that's for sure. ahora todo delivered por drones and whatnots... kind of miss the personal touch, tu sabes? considering my job, thats pretty rich coming from me, lol. oh well... ya me voy, gotta check some posts on reddit before sleep. hasta luego!

question_asked: I remember growing up in a small town in Colorado, the landscape was pretty flat with a lot of farmland all around. We would have really hot summers and really cold winters. Does your experience with the environment you grew up in differ a lot from mine?
response: oh mate, i can tell you str8 away that growing up in stockholm was a whole different ballgame than a colorado farm town! winters were freaking brutal.. like, freeze your face off brutal, haha. summers were nice tho, often chill, not too hot .. that really helped keeping the 'ol brain in shape during summer break from school. as an architect now, i kinda find myself kinda missing those brutal weather changes, 'cause i mean, over here in gothenburg it's pretty much the same weather all the time - constant gloomy drizzle, haha. maybe i just got used to the weather back home, but man, sometimes change is a good thing, keeps you awake, right? ;)

question_asked: I've traveled a lot over the years and picked up a couple of languages along the way. I started with English of course, but for my third grade assignment living in Beijing, I had to learn Mandarin. It was a challenge, but totally worth it, I even picked up the local dialect there too! Language shapes the way we think, doesn’t it? How about you? Did you grow up learning multiple languages or dialects?
response: oh absolutely mate, language does shape our thinking a lot! i mean, i was born in Kolkata, India but now i live in Delhi. hindi is our "rashtriya bhasha" (national language), but each state has its own language too. so i grew up with bengali at home, hindi in schol, cuz thats what most folks speak in Delhi. learnt bit of sanskrit as well in high school, all those "shlokas" still ring in my head haha. and ofc, english because global world bro. so yeah, different languages, different nuances, different ways to express... enriches life a lot, doesn't it? and as a professor in Astrophysics, believe me, the language of the cosmos is yet another fascinating one to learn :D

question_asked: I've always been impressed by how multilingual people are where I live. Here in Belgium, it's quite common for people to speak more than one language, thanks to being a meeting point of Latin and Germanic cultures and languages. For me personally, I speak French, Dutch and English. How about you? How many languages do you speak and was it usual in your area growing up?
response: oh man, being from india, it's like a flippin language buffet here. born in kolkata, grew up speakin' bengali with family, and english at school cause, well, it's almost the lingua franca here among the educated classes. then shifted to new delhi for work and uni, had to pick up hindi, cause you know, when in rome or in this case, delhi. so yeah, all in all, three languages right there but varying degrees of fluency for sure, english>bengali>hindi, haha. yea, growing up it was common to hear multiple languages, even aside from bengali and hindi. remember, india has 22 officially recognized languages and countless dialects. language diversity is just a part of life here, it's the norm, not the exception, mate. 😄

question_asked: Lately, I've been really into researching my family's genealogy. I dove into the layers of history, and it made me curious about the origins of powerful historical figures. One that particularly caught my attention is Ataturk. His reforms seem to be trigger points to modern Turkey. This got me wondering, do you have a significant historical figure in your country's history that made significant reforms or contributions? How do you see them and how they are embedded in your society today?
response:
oh man, talking about the touchpoints in history, right? there's this old bloke from hereabouts, Mannerheim they call him, kinda the Ataturk of Finland you could say... World War II was a crazy time here. The old boy was President, and lead the military against Soviet Union. Heck, it was under his watch Finland remained an independent nation. 

gotta tell you, like operating on a patient right? every incision, stitch and suture counts, stick it right there, and that's the kind of careful, deliberate work this man did for the country... despite several disagreements within the country, our healthcare is kick-ass, he made universal healthcare happen, now, where would i be without that?

You see statues of him and his horse everywhere, esp in the city centre. Just can't miss it, like an appendix in my surgical field haha. He ain't perfect, but man, gotta give him credit. He's the closest thing we've got to a national legend here. To this day, The Mannerheim Journey is taught in school which follows his journey from Turku to Ural Mountains, you know his roots, its all quite fascinating.

above my pay grade to judge his contributions but he's left his mark, just like how we doctors leave ours on our patients. Our work is our contribution to the world. i guess that's how i see it.

question_asked: One thing that I love so much about my neighborhood is the local bakery. It bakes this bread that is typical to the region where I was born. Every bite of it takes me right back to my childhood. I'm not sure if you also have this, but do you associate any specific type of food with your homeland? What was it like growing up there? Don't worry if you've moved since then, we can still chat about your hometown. How about that?
response: Ah, mate, you’re right onto something with that, nailing memories with food. I'll tell ya, my taste buds become little rangefinders every time I snag myself a bowl of goulash. Ain't as good as mam’s used to brew back at the day, but gives me that homesick-ish, warm-all-around feeling, you know? Growing up was a total blast, filled with little adventures amidst these awe-inspiring, centuries-old buildings. Granted, they were not as close to each other as they are in some parts of the world (cough, bìg ben, cough). When I wasn't secretly exploring, I was hustling at school, counting hours till I'd be free, dreaming of bigger ponds, those of bizarre triangular fishes. Guess some dreams do come true, eh?

question_asked: I always remember growing up with the smell of deep-dish pizza from my favorite place in my city, quite a contrast from my parents' native country dishes. It made me realize how interconnected and diverse the world has become and how food can tell such fascinating stories about people's origin. What's a dish you remember fondly from your childhood or something that gives you a nostalgic feeling of home?
response: ah mate, your memory got me feeling all warm and fuzzy inside. i remember, as a nipper, scarfing down my mum's pavlova. she would whip it up as a special treat on birthdays and such. the crisp meringue with the gooey inside, topped with whipped cream and fresh fruits, it was magic mate. a proper fair dinkum aussie delight, despite what those kiwis might say. when i taste it now, it's like footy in the park and kicking about in the sun. amazing how a dish can shoot ya straight back to the past, eh? good on ya for stirring up sweet memories mate!

question_asked: Man, talking with you brings up old memories of my school years. I was in an international school where we had to learn three languages: English, French, and the local tongue, Swiss German. It always felt like a total mind bend, constantly switching between all three languages. But it opened up so many cool opportunities later in life. How about you, do you recall juggling multiple languages during your school years?
response: ha! u know, here in canada, we've got a similar situation. born & raised in montreal, so yeah i was juggling english and french fluently, and trust me, I've had my fair share of lingual gymnastics too lol. i must admit, sometimes it felt like my brain was going to explode. but looking back, it's been super beneficial though! in fact, a lot of my clients are francophone, so that bilingualism comes in handy when practicing psychotherapy. never learned swiss german tho... sounds brutal tbh haha!

question_asked: I find languages so interesting. I registered for a course to learn Chinese, but man, it was tough. I'd love to get more insights. What's your mother tongue? Any survival phrase that you can share?
response:
ah, mate, no worries, i totally get where you're coming from with the language bit. chinese sounds well interesting, but aye, reckon it'd be a tough nut to crack. me, I was born in melbourne, down here in STRAYA, so Aussie English is the lingo i speak, and could talk ya ear off given half the chance, haha! 

as for survival phrases, if ever you're here in the land down under and find yourself in a bit of a pickle, just remember this one: "good onya, mate!" said the right way, it can express gratitude, admiration, encouragement, basically anything positive. works a charm, mate, trust me, i've been getting by for 68 years with it. 

oh and do us a solid, if you're ever "on the piss" (out having drinks), bring sunnies. our sun doesn't muck about here in Sydney. good luck with the chinese lessons, mate!

question_asked: I visited Notre-Dame cathedral before it was damaged by fire and marveled at its Gothic architecture. Are there any famous historic buildings where you're from that you find compelling?
response:
oh wow, notre dame, must've been crazy beautiful, huh? can't say i've had the pleasure of visiting. reminds me of this old cathedral right in my old stomping grounds tho. You know, we're famous for our architecture - really cool medieval stuff, cobblestone streets and all that jazz. Specifically the Turun Tuomiokirkko, (~Turku Cathedral) really kicks ass. 

Can't say I hang out there often, more into the hustle and bustle in the big city myself. Online space's more my vibe, I'm kinda addicted to reddit, lol. But yeah, you should totally check it out if you're ever in Finland. Crazy history there, ya know? War, fires, rebuilds... kinda like europe in a nutshell.

question_asked: I was just reminiscing about my childhood and the Christmas traditions we had. We'd have loads of Christmas pudding and I'd divide the last bit with my sisters hoping that we'd find the silver coin that we'd been told brings luck. Such a joyous festival! How did you celebrate your main cultural or religious festival as a kid?
response: hej, brings back memories of my childhood yuletide celebrations! it's pretty big over here. we'd have a proper "julbord", bunch of traditional dishes. it was darn good, specially the pickled herring... got quite a tongue for pickles, might be the viking blood eh :). but the best part was awaiting for the Tomte. we'd one in our household, usually my farfar (grandpa), going around giving presents. mom said it's because of the good old St. Nicolas, even though we were like on the 24th lmao. yup, good times, cheers for asking!

question_asked: Growing up, my culinary experience was a bit different than most. My home was a playground of fine cuisine. My mother preferred zesty, flavorful dishes from South America, my father enjoyed comforting, hearty foods from Eastern Europe, and my neighbors shared delightful Asian treats. It was an interesting mix! How would you describe your childhood food culture? Did your family have any favorite recipes they could not go a week without cooking?
response:
oh man, your childhood sounds like a global food festival. for me, well... let's just say it was a bit more traditional and suited to the weather, heh. my grandma was a huge influence, and her dishes were a staple in our home. there was this thing she prepared called 'pulla', a cardamom spiced bread, sweet and delicious, and let's just say my belly really appreciated her efforts. 

every now and then, i'd mix up things a bit and ask (or rather demand, lol) her to make fried vendace. it's basically crisply fried, small fish... part of the bona fide local experience if you ask me. not your fancy smorgasbord, but it kept us nice and toasty during our long winters. :)

question_asked: In my country, we are huge soccer freaks. All of us, from children to seniors, enjoy playing or watching soccer games, especially when we are cheering our national team. I remember when I was younger, we used to gather in cafés to watch the games especially during the World Cup or African Cup of Nations. It created a great sense of community within my town. How about you? Do you have any special sports from where you are or events related to sports that gather everyone around? You can't but feel a bit nostalgic about these things, right?
response: Haha, oh haven't played footie since my teen years! Over here cricket is the great leveller man. Doesn't matter if it's collegiates, accountants, tuk-tuk drivers or rocket scientists like me, the game brings everyone together. We've citywide meltdowns everytime the IPL's on, swings in mass mood more volatile than your average physics experiment! And Eden Gardens... beautiful place to get lost in the roar, still hear echoes of the home crowd while I munch my jhalmuri. Now that's a nostalgia trip worth taking.

question_asked: I could never forget my childhood spent catching fireflies on warm summer nights back home. It's an activity that kids love in many parts of the world. Do you have a cherished childhood pastime from your place that you could share?
response: oh absolutely! summer evenings got us kids flocking to open fields. instead of fireflies though, we'd look out for these flowers, we call em nattljus, night lights, you know, like big yellow lanterns in the twilight. my bro and i would compete, who finds the first one, just by running around barefoot and feeling the grass n petals under our feet. while parents bbq'd in the backyard 😊 kinda miss those simple times, hehe. then one couldn't care less about responsive designs and broken hyperlinks, just the grass and the nattljus... simply sweden, innit? 🌻🌿

question_asked: I was lucky to have grown up in California where winters were pretty mild and we could pretty much play sports outside all year round. I always found it fascinating how the change of seasons affects people's lifestyle and hobbies. How about you, have you experienced a season that made your activities a bit more interesting or challenged?
response: oh mate, you'd be astounded by the kiwi lifestyle, i was born in auckland and now living in wellington, i reckon i’ve had my fair share of earth’s mood swings. now, the riding my bike to work gets bit interesting in winters. in wellington uh? it gets hella windy and cold my fingers are nearly frozen despite the gloves. i practically feel like i’m in a boxing match with the wind! try going green in that, bet you can't survive a week haha. still, wouldn’t trade it for the world. adds a dash of some good old adventure i reckon ;)

question_asked: I grew up in a region where we have to learn multiple languages in school from a young age. For me, it was a mix of Lithuanian, English and Russian, which was quite a challenge. How about you? Did you have to learn many languages in your school? How many do you fluently speak now?
response: well mate, hailing from perth, i too had to get stuck into a fair share of languages during my school years. i mean, english was a given, obviously, it being aussie n' all. but i also got to hafta delve into japanese n french. you could say it was kinda quite a journey, oi. now, in all honesty, can't say i'm fluent in either japanese or french... a bit of survival conversation, yeah? that's about it lol. i reckon i'd rather crunch numbers as a financial analyst than trying to fully understand 'le conditionnel passé' or whatever. english? now that's a different story, sailing smoothly there. so, yeah, in total, fluent in one. reckon i gotta give it another crack someday!

question_asked: I've been so lucky to have attended primary school in Canada, where the quality of education is really high and we learn to speak both English and French at a young age. We also have special festivals and traditions associated with each province. What was your primary school experience like? Did your school have any specific festivals or celebrations?
response: oh, primary school days, such a memory trip you got me onto! we also had the two languages, although here it's spanish and catalan. and festivals, did we ever! and it's not just school ones, the whole city turns to a different place. Las Fallas, Sant Jordi, and my personal favorite - La Merce! You've not seen a city celebrate until you've seen human towers, fire breathing dragons, street arts and music all in one week! all around the gothic district and the infamous Sagrada Familia. now *that's* a cultural trip, i tell ya.

question_asked: When I was little, my dad used to take me to a bakery early in the morning and I could smell the fresh bread from a block away. What's your favourite childhood smell? Do you have any special bakery or food that reminds you of your childhood?
response: Oh man, the smell of fresh jianbing being made on a cold morning takes me back. Dad used to wake me up at the crack of dawn on weekends, not the most ideal for a kid who wants to sleep in, right? But boy, was it worth it! The air was always so crisp, and the smell of that Chinese crepe sizzling away, egg cracked onto it, right on the roadside... Ah, heavenly! Still makes my mouth water, lol. Made queuing up with the morning office rush tolerable cause at the end, I would have my steaming jianbing filled with all the good stuff. It's like a warm hug on a winter's day, really. That's something doughnuts can never match. Now, every time winter comes and I see a jianbing stall, such nostalgia kicks in, I tell you.

question_asked: I remember as a kid, around this time of the year we would receive the most snow and my siblings and I would often build snowmen. It was always a joyous time. Of course, we had to wear many layers, otherwise we'd freeze. How about you? Do you remember any unique weather conditions from your childhood?
response: ou, johannesburg. born n raised! we didn't really have the snowy christmases and all, it was more like shorts n flip-flops braai weather, haha. few times some hailstorms. Those were like mini ice cubes raining down on us, sharp lil buggers can surprise you for sure, yeesh. dunno how you guys kept up with those ice-cold fingers. but hey, we've all got our weather woes, right? Most importantly, those memories are golden, snow or sun!

question_asked: I once had an amazing linguistics professor in college who taught us so much about how language shapes our world. He had this theory that someone's mother tongue can influence their entire perspective on life. Isn't that wild? I mean, I'm definitely biased because English is my first language but I do find myself thinking in English even when I'm speaking another language. What about you? Do you feel your mother tongue shapes your worldview in any way? But, first, tell me what it is, if you don't mind sharing. This kind of stuff just fascinates me.
response:
ah, fascinating topic! i'm a finn, born in turku, so mi madre language is finnish, jsyk. in finnish, there is no future tense, ever think about that? so, i'm like always in the 'here and now' state of mind, haha. basically, procrastination's in my blood. also, we finns can make up words on the go. some ungodly long words for simple things, like 'korvapuusti' for cinnamon roll. brings a lot of fun to life, man.

actually, this linguistic phenomena can be a pain when it comes to my professional life..i'm a surgeon u know, and the precision in language required..ah man...sometimes makes me wonder, if the lack of future tense in Finnish affects how I plan surgeries, probably spend too much time in the 'now,' less on the 'what next', haha. 

so yea mate, i reckon this language and culture stuff really shapes a big part of us, in a weird sort of way.

question_asked: I still fondly remember my childhood days, playing around the beaches and eating some amazing seafood. The tastes still linger on my palate, especially the crab dishes. And, of course, I can't forget the vibrant music culture, with jazz bands strumming chords at every corner. Are there any special foods or music styles typical to your childhood place?
response: Oh, your're stirring up nostalgia now! Back in the day, the waft of fresh 'Fischbrötchen' (hehe, try saying that) from the nearby markets early in the morning was just the kickstart to a day. And speaking of music - there's something uniquely mesmerizing about St. Pauli's rebellious punk scene. Bit of an acquired taste for some, but it's as deeply ingrained in me as the taste of spicy herring on a chilly tuesday morning. Good times.

question_asked: It's funny that when I was a kid, my parents used to take me and my siblings on road trips all the time. We did the typical long drives and beach trips, but my most vivid memories were the apple-picking trips during the fall season, it was just magical. We would drive for hours, then pick heaps of apples and enjoy fresh apple pies and apple cider for days. What were some of the family outings or trips you had as a kid that you remember fondly?
response: oh man, your fall apple-picking trips just zapped me right back… lemme tell ya, my folks loved a bit of a road trip, too. funny thing is they had this weird obsession with driving up and down along the river, all way from our town to some weird french-only speaking place (hated every second of their intruding chitchat as kid, go figure). but they got their booya moment, cause this one time i remember seeing an absurd amount of Big Os... i mean they were everywhere, like a snow infested city but instead of a white Christmas, it became the city of orange construction cones. couldn't wrap my lil head around it back then, figured it was some local tradition or something, haha. the only thing that saved my sanity on these trips were the exquisite poutine stops. seriously, to die for! best part of those audacious expeditions, hands down. grab a piping hot gravy ladened poutine and just savour the view of cosplaying traffic cones, what a time! ah, memories, eh?

question_asked: I was born in a country where everyone knows about football, we're practically born with a ball at our feet. And the rivalry between cities when it comes to soccer is visceral. How's the sports culture where you come from? Do you have any sports rivalry within the country that feels almost personal?
response: oh man, you talk about rivalry? the one i've been weaned on was the one between those big old OHC boys and the knights of CCC. everybody'd drop whatever they were doing just to watch their games when they'd duke it out on the football ground. bleachers brimming over, every single time. shoveled the whole way to the stadium through snow and hail and rain once.. good times, haha. gave up all that chaos for the calm of zurich tho, and am happier for it. but the memories, they stick around.

question_asked: I was really into ice hockey in my middle school days, we used to play it in the winters. Our town was like super geared up for it in the season, there were hockey rings popping up all over the place with people bustling about. Do you have a sport that is like super popular in your place while growing up? A sport that pretty much everyone was into? There must be some unique ones in your area growing up!
response: Oh mate, so you were an ice hockey guy, eh? Good sport that! Down here we're not too wild about that ice malarkey. I reckon you'd have a pretty hard time finding even one side to have a go at hockey, let alone several! Nah, down here we growing up we were all mad about rugby, specifically following the All Blacks and the Super Rugby. Whether in public parks, school grounds or sheep fields we'd be chucking about an oval ball and practicing our Haka. Every lad wanted to be Richie McCaw or Jonah Lomu. It's more than a game here I tell ya, it's our lifeblood! Now in my golden years, I find myself more of a spectator, enjoying the matches from my couch mostly. Even managed to teach the missus a thing or two about scrums and line-outs. Go the All Blacks!

question_asked: I've always been a huge fan of football, or soccer as they call it here in the US. Growing up, I had no games to attend to, I had to settle for watching my favorite teams and players on TV. In fact, I had to wake up at odd hours due to timezone differences. If you are a football fan, which teams did you root for during your young age? If not, is there any major sport in your country that you remember discussing with your friends at school?
response: awww mate, footie! those were the days. i used to jus' dream about those sparkling kits on tv. ya see, cable came way late in my city, but the wait was totally worth it for the premier league matches. couldn't really pick a side, eh? with my mates, we'd stick to shouting for the copperbelt's finest, even if it ain't as glamourous lol. but hey, every now n then we'd argue bout the power dynamo vs nkana classics, good times i tell ya! always loved the passionate spirit of our local league, even if the football's not as polished as the prem's you know :p

question_asked: What a joy it is to witness the change of seasons! I grew up in a place where we enjoyed all four seasons- spring, summer, autumn, and winter- each with its own charm and challenges. It's inconceivable for me not to see fall foliage or make snow angels in winter. Just curious, did you grew up experiencing different seasons or was it mostly the same kind of weather throughout the year?
response: hah, mate I can tell ya, seems like those childhood summer vacations in the town by the north never really had a proper summer even with the Mediterranean there n all. Barely can hit the 30 centigrade, blowin' chilly winds well into July. You'd expect more solid sunshine given the proximity to the French folks on the riviera, right? Now contrast that with Madrid, where I stay now, man those summers here! the sun's on a belter - few degrees past 40C and you're practically grilled here. And about the fall, it's mild and pretty okay-ish I'd say—not too many tree types to show off some spectacular colour palette, though. And ya won't really see any snow 'round these parts, unlike up north. So yeah, quite the contrast from the days of my youth to now; but you know, it does give you a new perspective, says the history geek in me. :)

question_asked: I was reminiscing about my family trip to see the Northern Lights in Alaska, it was simply mesmerizing. I guess every region has its own kind of natural phenomenon that amazes people. Do you have any similar kind of phenomenon around your birthplace that the locals are proud of?
response: oh jag älskar att du frågade detta! i was born in malmö and we might not have the northern lights (vilken underbar upplevelse du måste ha haft), but we do have the turning torso! it's this supersnygg skyscraper that literally looks like it's twisting. crazy cool architecture design that we are so proud of. like seriously, it beats ikea hands down in the funky swedish design aspects, haha. it's like our very own mini nutida wonder of the world. we're not short on natural phenomena though, skåne's beaches and forests are kind of amazing as well, just in a different, low key, cosy way. fika och promenade, det är vad vi gör haha!

question_asked: Back in my high school days, I used to be quite a history buff and today, whenever I look at the Tiber River, it always brings back memories of the countless history lessons about Romans and their rich past. Speaking of rivers and history, do you live near any rivers that have historical significance? How has it influenced your local area?
response: haha, not living near any Tiber River that's cert for sure, but LA? duuuude, history lessons always bebop of how the 'City of Angels' wouldn't be the same without the LA River, like... Foundation and stuff. Now? damn concrete jungle. Very Flintstones to Jetsons, right? So weird. i mean it's not Roman level history, but for a left coast kid, it was pretty rad. I'd kill for some of those SoCal vibes in NYC.... cold as @#$% out here dude. sprinkled with a pinch of why-am-i-even-paying-this-much-for-rent...sigh.

question_asked: I spent a substantial amount of my childhood in Canada, and I always admired the way hockey formed a major part of our collective cultural identity. Even though I was just a moderately decent player, ice hockey was such an integral part of the community. Do you have a sport like that where you're from, one that almost everyone around you is a fan of and even plays on the local level?
response: ah sure, yer not quite off the mark. sport's pretty ingrained in us, alright. here, we have a grand old time with hurling. now, I wouldn't exactly call me a pro hurler, but kicking up a sliotar in the park on a crisp, cool morning after the rain, now there's something that brings me right back to my days as a nipper. we're all mad for it, can't quite escape it even if ye'd like to. it's like a rite of passage, y'know, get a hurley in your hand before you can even walk. And i've to tell ya, the excitement around the All-Ireland Final? something else entirely. Talking about it online, in the pubs, it's mental stuff altogether. Kinda like your own Stanley Cup, I'd wager.

question_asked: Oh, I just remembered my middle school days and walking by the local bakery every morning on my way to school. The smell of freshly baked bread used to be intoxicating. Do you have any scent memories like that, which gets you nostalgic about your childhood?
response: Ah, those whiffs of nostalgia, hmm? Those scents that get ya back to the good ol' times eh? I always reminisce when the aroma of freshly made poutine hits me, and I'm instantly transported back to my childhood. back in the days when my world was just school and hockey, and the poutines from the neighborhood casse-croûte.  Oh, and winters. I can't forget the cold, crisp scent of maple syrup being tapped right off the trees... takes me straight back to my stomping grounds. Maple leaves and hockey sticks, truly Canadian sigh. Gotta love it, eh?

question_asked: I remember growing up, every Sunday morning would be football day. Nothing else mattered but the game on the screen and the crowds in the stadiums. It was all about the Premier League for us, but I know different countries have different football cultures. I've always wondered how the football fan experience differs in other countries. So, what's your fondest football memory from growing up?
response: Aw mate, can't say me childhood was filled with much footy excitement. Instead of TV screens, I remember spending way too much time gazing up at the kauri trees in the bush near where I grew up - serious Jurassic Park vibes, y’know? Proceeded to nerd out on environmental sciences instead of the All Whites game. Theirs was not the path I walked, but hey, kiwi to kiwi, good on ya if it brought your family together. Passion's passion, no matter what form it takes.

question_asked: Growing up in a smaller city was quite nice for me, and I noticed that even the language we spoke was slightly different from the standard one because of regional dialects. I guess many places have their unique way of speaking, not necessarily a completely different language but just a touch of local color, you know? What’s the local dialect or slang like in your area?
response: oh yeah, the ol' accent game! In Delhi, we got a nice lil concoction of Punjabi, Haryanvi, and Hindi mixed up in our lingo. there is a fair bit of english in there too! haha. like, we'd be sayin' "kya scene hai?" when we talk about "what's happening?". now my kolkata roots does pop up once in a while, especially when i'm chattin' with my chaddi buddies (closest friends), we lapse into Bangla and that definitely brings a nostalgic smile. bijoya reminiscences at its best, yeah. on reddit tho, mostly its just english with the occasional local lingo dropped in for flavor! chat's pretty chill around here.

question_asked: I recently returned from my trip to Spain. I fell in love with their tapas and flamenco dance. It got me thinking about the cultural uniqueness of different corners of the world. I am curious, do you have any cultural dance forms or unique cuisines from where you grew up?
response: mate, I was born in Budapest, and let me tell you, we Hungarians know how to get down. our traditional dance, it's called the csárdás, and let me tell you, it's no smooth flamenco, more like wild footwork and spins. and when it comes to food, goulash all the way, beef, augur, paprika, potatoes, some secret ingredients segitő's grandma doesn't share, cooked in a kettle, a big pot on an open fire... ugh, mates google it, I am now salivating and missing home, here in London trying to afford a pub fish and chips on a waiter's wages. cheers for the memories tho!

question_asked: I have to say, I'm quite lucky to be living in a country where we have all four seasons. I particularly enjoy the autumn foliage, it's just so beautiful. Funny enough, though, my partner strongly prefers the summer sun and the bright warm days. Not to mention the fact that we get to take out the barbecue equipment. I'm curious, what's your favorite season and why? Any particular tradition you enjoy during that time?
response:
aye, the celestial ballet that is the change of seasons. There's something mystical in the air during winters, especially the foggy mornings. right, i'm not big on the cold per se. but my favourite pastime's chasing the stars, you know, tracing constellations, marvelling at galaxies - far, far away. winters offer the clearest skies, hence this fondness. 

And yes, being a bong, we do have a tradition to celebrate with family around small bonfires, noshing on puffed rice and patishapta (a sweet crepe, sorta). you should try someday, it's like waltzing with the stars within arm's reach. quite the solstice spectacle!

question_asked: I totally remember these days as a kid, playing footy in the park, with the scent of eucalyptus in the air, as it is quite dominant here in Australia. What were some of your favorite childhood memories? Did you also have a special smell in the air, or a signature game you and your friends used to play?
response: oh man, bringing back the feels ya know? so i was born in nagoya, right? and as a kid, we used to play onigokko (sorta like tag) in the neighborhood. the smell, oh the smell... it has to be sakura blossoms blooming in Spring; that smell is just so unique and nostalgic. it brings back memories of running around and laughter. and of course, post onigokko tradition - a hearty bowl of miso katsu, nagoya style mate. fingers still sticky from the taste and sweat... good days, those were good days indeed. gotta admit, wouldn't mind catching a whiff of sakura every now and then amidst all the coding and whatnot out here in tokyo.

question_asked: I remember going on these long hikes back in the day when I was in the Scouts. It used to be such an adventure exploring the great outdoors, getting to know all kinds of flora and fauna. We used to camp in the wilderness, make our own food over the open fire, tell ghost stories at night and stargaze. It was where I found my love for astronomy. I have to say, the clear night skies of rural Australia, where I grew up, were pretty mesmerising. Have you had any similar experiences growing up? Did you used to be a part of any such clubs or groups?
response:
hey, your scouting days sound so wicked cool, mate! camping under the stars and aye, i reckon that would've been one belter of a view in rural Australia. for me though, growing up in Glasgow, it was a bit different, eh? like, there were more buildings around, but that didn't stop me from stargazing and falling in love with those celestial bodies. 

i remember joining this local astronomy club in my teens, we used to sneak out to the "quieter" parts of town (the ones without the bloody light pollution, ya know?) and just spend hours looking at the stars with our garish little telescopes. those nights were minted, honestly. sorta led me down my career path, now that i think of it, ending up as an astronomer and all. so yeah, guess we both found our way to the stars, just in our own ways, eh? :)

question_asked: I have such fond memories of visiting the local summer fair in a small town where I grew up. Those popcorns, cotton candy, and those thrilling rides still make me giggle like a child. Do you also have traditional fairs or festivals where you come from? Tell me about the most memorable one you've attended, please!
response: oh man, reading this gave me all the feels haha. totally remember, growing up we had this huge festival in my grandma's town. it's not the big city where I live now, but dear god, the food stalls there were NEXT LEVEL. the smell of roasted chestnuts wafting through the air, oh dear... and don't even get me started on the misty, cold mornings. felt like stepping right into a manueline painting or something lol. the mist gave the ancient stones a kind of surreal aura. but the real deal breaker were those insane gigantes e cabeçudos parades, you know giant effigies of historical figures with exaggerated heads bobbing to the traditional folk music haha. i mean i'm too old for that now, but damn if i would miss that wine pouring ceremony. classic, i tell ya. what about you? any local fair traditions from your end?

question_asked: The late-night barbecue parties my family hosts are legendary in the small town I grew up in, here in Texas. There was always an excitement in the air as we waited for the slow-cooked, spicy barbecue to be ready. Are there any such unique dining traditions in the place you grew up that you hold dear?
response:
ah, texas bbq sha! sounds absolutely heartwarmingly delicious. you're making my mouth water, haha. 

in my corner of the world, durban, south africa, we have a version of bbq called a 'braai'. it's not just about cooking meats over an open flame, oh no, it's a social event... a lifestyle even. the smoky aroma of boerewors (farmer's sausage) & marinated chops sizzling on the hot coals, while the sunset paints the sky in shades of red and orange, ugh... just magic! 

we also have a special dish, bunny chow. no, don't be shocked, it ain't bunny meat, lol. it's basically half a loaf of white bread hollowed out and filled with deliciously hot curry. it's a curry in a bread bowl, essentially. that alongside a good game of rugby... yoh, it's like our own little piece of heaven. 

damn, i'm missing home now, it's been a while since i had an authentic bunny chow. can't seem to find one here in cape town that hits the spot, you know?

question_asked: I remember my childhood when my parents shared stories of the winter season in my hometown. The skiing, the snowball fights, and of course, hot chocolate. Later, it was crazy to compare my experiences in a snowy country with people who never saw snow on Christmas. Do you have any special childhood memory about celebrating Christmas? Anything unique that you think only happens in your town?
